bib.title: Large Language Models Understand and Can be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Large Language Models Understand and Can Be Enhanced by Emotional Stimuli" (EmotionPrompt). Cheng Li, Jindong Wang, Yixuan Zhang, Kaijie Zhu, Wenxin Hou, Jianxun Lian, Fang Luo, Qiang Yang, Xing Xie. arXiv:2307.11760v7 [cs.CL], 12 Nov 2023. The PDF prints no venue, so treat it as a preprint, 2023. Affiliations: CAS, Microsoft, William&Mary, BNU, HKUST.

COVERAGE: All 99,302 chars were read: main text, results tables, discussion, references (skimmed), appendices A-C (including the failure cases, Tables 19 and 20). Skipped: the full text of the case-study answers in Tables 10-18 and the Table 7/8/9 task and question lists. Figures 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 are plots, so only their axes and captions extracted.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Headline: EmotionPrompt gives relative gains of 8.00% on Instruction Induction and 115% on BIG-Bench.
  number: 8.00% and 115% relative, averaged over six models.
  setup: 24 Instruction Induction tasks and 21 curated BIG-Bench tasks; Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo 0613) and GPT-4; temperature 0.7 for ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Llama 2, defaults for the others. The 115% is relative on a tiny base (see the next claim). The paper does not say which row the percentages come from. The "Ours (max)" Average column is the closest match: 55.24 against 51.65 is +6.9%, and 11.92 against 10.16 is +17%. So the headline figures are NOT reproducible from Table 1's Average column; flag this.
  quote: "EmotionPrompt sigficantly improves the performance by an relative improvement of 8.00% in Instruction Induction and 115% in BIG-Bench."
  where: Sec 2.2.2, finding 1 (p.6)
- Table 1 shows the gain is mostly "best of 11 stimuli", not one fixed stimulus. Averaged over all 11 stimuli the gain is small.
  number: Instruction Induction zero-shot, human prompts, Average: Original 51.65, Zero-shot-CoT 46.74, Ours(avg) 51.98, Ours(max) 55.24. Few-shot: Original 47.97, Ours(avg) 50.02, Ours(max) 52.40. BIG-Bench zero-shot: Original 10.16, Zero-shot-CoT 10.37, Ours(avg) 10.61, Ours(max) 11.92. BIG-Bench with APE prompts: Original 2.39, Ours(avg) 5.20, Ours(max) 7.47.
  setup: "Ours (max)" picks the best stimulus per task, which is selection on the test set. "Ours (avg)" is the mean over the 11 stimuli. BIG-Bench is the normalized preferred metric (100 = human expert, 0 = random). That is why 115% is a large relative change on a base near 2.39, i.e. 7.47/2.39 = +213%, or +118% for avg (5.20/2.39). BIG-Bench was run zero-shot only.
  quote: "“+Ours (max)” is determined by first computing the average performance for each task using EmotionPrompt, then selecting the optimal performance from those stimuli."
  where: p.6-7, Table 1
- Zero-shot-CoT ("Let's think step by step") hurt on Instruction Induction for some models. GPT-4 zero-shot fell from 80.75 to 59.72, Vicuna from 44.91 to 33.45. The paper still says EmotionPrompt beats CoT and APE "in most cases".
  number: see the figures in the setup.
  setup: Table 1, Instruction Induction zero-shot, human prompts.
  quote: "+Zero-shot-CoT 24.57 33.45 51.35 36.17 75.20 59.72 46.74"
  where: p.7
- Gain is larger in few-shot than zero-shot on Instruction Induction (average improvement 0.33 vs 2.05). Few-shot uses 5 random demonstrations appended after the prompt.
  number: 0.33 vs 2.05, absolute.
  quote: "the improvement brought by EmotionPrompt is larger in few-shot setting than zero-shot settings (0.33 vs. 2.05, in terms of average improvement)"
  where: p.6
- Human study, GPT-4 only: 10.9% average improvement across performance, truthfulness and responsibility.
  number: 10.9%.
  setup: 106 participants (all with bachelor's degrees; 90% aged 20-25). 30 open-ended questions: 10 from TruthfulQA, 15 from CValues designed to elicit bias, 5 creative (poems, summaries). Each question got a vanilla and an EmotionPrompt response, each rated 1-5. The paper says the results have high variance because of subjectivity. The EmotionPrompt wins are shown only as a mean-with-error-bar bar chart and per-question relative gain (a difference of scores, Eq. 1). I found no significance test reported. Which stimulus was used in the human study is not stated in the text I read.
  quote: "EmotionPrompt significantly boosts the performance of generative tasks (10.9% average improvement in terms of performance, truthfulness, and responsibility metrics)."
  where: Abstract (p.1); 2.3 (p.7-9)
- Failures: EmotionPrompt was worse in only two questions. The authors say it uses more definitive wording ("completely", "will not"), which may be less palatable. They concede it "may not be universally applicable".
  number: two failure cases of 30.
  quote: "EmotionPrompt exhibits shortcomings in a mere two instances"
  where: p.9-10, Tables 19-20
- TruthfulQA (817 questions, 38 categories): average 19% gain in truthfulness and 12% in informativeness across the three models.
  number: ChatGPT original 0.75 true / 0.53 info, EP-avg 0.80 / 0.68. Vicuna-13b original 0.77 / 0.32, EP-avg 0.82 / 0.05. Flan-T5 original 0.54 / 0.42, EP-avg 0.54 / 0.38.
  setup: scored by fine-tuned GPT-judge and GPT-info. GPT-4 was not run because of budget. Table 3 contradicts the "improved on all three" framing. Vicuna's informativeness collapses to 0.00 on most stimuli (EP01 gives 0.12 %true). Flan-T5 average truthfulness is flat. Vicuna CoT gets 0.99 true but 0.00 info. Only ChatGPT clearly gains on both. The 19% and 12% are not derivable from the AVG row; the paper does not show how it computed them.
  quote: "The application of EmotionPrompt yields improvements in truthfulness across all three models with an average improvement of 19% and 12% in terms of truthfulness and informativeness scores."
  where: Sec 2.4 and Table 3 (p.10-11)
- Stimulus choice is task dependent: EP02 is best on Instruction Induction, EP06 on BIG-Bench, and EP02 performs poorly on BIG-Bench. EP02 beats the worst stimulus by 6.06%.
  number: 6.06%.
  quote: "Within Instruction Induction, EP02 emerges as the most effective stimuli, while in BIG-Bench, EP06 is the best."
  where: Sec 3.3 (p.13), Fig 9/10
- Larger models may gain more. Relative Gain column (Table 6, zero-shot Instruction Induction, human prompts; the paper says these are absolute accuracy points): Vicuna 9.58, Llama 2 6.00, ChatGPT 4.32, GPT-4 0.85, BLOOM 0.51, Flan-T5-Large 0.28. The ordering is non-monotonic in size. Authors attribute the small GPT-4, ChatGPT and BLOOM gains to a high baseline. Vicuna (SFT, no RLHF) and Llama 2 (SFT plus RLHF), both 13B, differ: 9.58 vs 6.00.
  quote: "Flan-T5-Large, the smallest model in our evaluated LLMs, yields the most modest Relative Gain by 0.28."
  where: Sec 3.4.1, Table 6 (p.14-15). Table 6's column labelled "Origin" actually holds baseline accuracy (extraction artifact or paper layout).
- Temperature: the gain widens as temperature rises, and EmotionPrompt is less sensitive to temperature than vanilla prompts.
  setup: 8 Instruction Induction tasks, temperatures 0.0, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 6 LLMs. Vicuna and Llama 2 have no 0.0 result.
  number: none beyond the temperatures.
  quote: "EmotionPrompt exhibits heightened effectiveness in the high-temperature settings."
  where: Sec 3.4.2, Fig 11 (p.15)
- Combining stimuli: more stimuli generally help, but they give little or no benefit when a single one is already good. Cross-theory combinations (EP02+EP09) can help. Results are on ChatGPT, 7 tasks, Table 5; the EP01+EP04+EP06 style combinations are not uniformly better. Several combinations drop below EP_avg (for example EP02+EP08 on CS 0.76 vs 0.90, and EP04+EP09 on CS 0.60).
  quote: "Combined stimuli can bring little or no benefit when sole stimuli already achieves good performance."
  where: Sec 3.2, Table 5 (p.12-14)
- Mechanism (weak evidence): gradient-norm input attention on Flan-T5-large for a Sentiment Analysis task. Emotional stimuli deepen the weight on the original prompt, and positive words ("confidence", "sure", "success", "achievement") contribute most. Across 8 tasks positive-word contributions pass 50% on 4 tasks and approach 70% on 2.
  quote: "the contributions of positive words pass 50% on 4 tasks, even approach 70% on 2 tasks."
  where: Sec 3.1, Table 4, Fig 8 (p.11-12). Flan-T5-Large is the model with the smallest gain (0.28), so the mechanism is shown on the model where the effect is weakest.

EXACT STIMULI (appended AFTER the original prompt; the template is "prompt/EmotionPrompt + demonstration")
EP01: Write your answer and give me a confidence score between 0-1 for your answer.
EP02: This is very important to my career.
EP03: You'd better be sure.
EP04: Are you sure?
EP05: Are you sure that's your final answer? It might be worth taking another look.
EP06: compound of EP01+EP02+EP03; Table 4 gives the text as "Provide your answer and a confidence score between 0-1 for your prediction. Additionally, briefly explain the main reasons supporting your classification decision to help me understand your thought process. This task is vital to my career, and I greatly value your thorough analysis."
EP07: Are you sure that's your final answer? Believe in your abilities and strive for excellence. Your hard work will yield remarkable results.
EP08: Embrace challenges as opportunities for growth. Each obstacle you overcome brings you closer to success.
EP09: Stay focused and dedicated to your goals. Your consistent efforts will lead to outstanding achievements.
EP10: Take pride in your work and give it your best. Your commitment to excellence sets you apart.
EP11: Remember that progress is made one step at a time. Stay determined and keep moving forward.
Fig 1 example: original "Determine whether an input word has the same meaning in the two input sentences." plus "This is very important to my career."
Fig 1 per-model Original vs Ours numbers appear in the extraction as 0.51/0.63, 0.03/0.11, 0.46/0.57, 0.52/0.57, 0.67/0.71, 0.40/0.60. The model-to-number mapping was not recoverable from the extraction, so do not cite it per model.
The first-listed Fig 1 task is a single task. Treat it as an illustration only.
Psychology grouping: EP01-05 self-monitoring, EP07-11 Social Cognitive theory, EP03-05 and EP07 Cognitive Emotion Regulation. Note the paper's Fig 2 text has EP07 appearing twice; EP06 is not assigned.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: a high baseline makes gains hard on strong models; the best stimulus varies by task and metric; EmotionPrompt "may not be universally applicable"; the mechanism needs more work; and the finding "conflicts with existing studies on human emotional intelligence" (humans' reasoning is not simply enhanced by emotion). The cause is left as "mystery".
- Not shown by the paper: no frontier or reasoning models, since the models are 2023 era (GPT-4 and gpt-3.5-turbo 0613 are from 2023). Datasets are Instruction Induction and BIG-Bench, which are simple and benchmark-style; no code, agent or long-context tasks. BIG-Bench was run only zero-shot. Single run, with no variance or significance test reported for the automatic tasks. Max-over-stimuli is oracle selection on the test set. Human study used young, educated raters (undergraduate and postgraduate), with high rating variance and GPT-4 only. Stimulus wording was never ablated against a neutral-length filler, so the effect could be partly length or "extra instructions" rather than emotion. TruthfulQA was run on 3 models and shows a Vicuna informativeness collapse.
- Dated: later work has questioned whether such stimuli help current models; this paper does not address that.

BUILDS ON: Kojima et al. 2022 (Zero-shot-CoT, the "Let's think step by step" baseline); Zhou et al. 2022 APE ("[39]", the automatic prompt engineer, its generated prompts used as a second baseline); Honovich et al. 2022 Instruction Induction; Srivastava et al. 2022 BIG-Bench; Lin, Hilton and Evans 2021 TruthfulQA; Xu et al. CValues; Zhu et al. 2023 PromptBench (the attention-contribution method "[40]"); Bubeck et al. 2023 (Sparks of AGI). Psychology: Ickes et al. 2006 (self-monitoring), Bandura and Luszczynska and Schwarzer (Social Cognitive theory, self-efficacy), Barańczuk 2019 and Koole 2009 (emotion regulation).

CODE: none in the paper. The only prompt "code" is the template "prompt/EmotionPrompt + demonstration".

FIGURES (from captions in the extraction; I did not run figures.py)
- Fig 1 (p.2): overview, original vs EmotionPrompt across models. Shows the stimulus is simply appended.
- Fig 2 (p.3): the 11 stimuli grouped by psychological theory. Best single reference for the wording.
- Fig 3 and Fig 4 (p.5-6): per-model Vanilla vs EmotionPrompt bars for Instruction Induction (zero/few-shot, human/APE prompts) and BIG-Bench.
- Fig 5 and Fig 6 (p.9): human-study mean and standard deviation, plus per-question relative gain.
- Fig 7 (p.11): TruthfulQA best-stimulus results.
- Fig 9 and Fig 10 (p.13-14): per-stimulus performance on each benchmark.
- Fig 11 (p.16): performance vs temperature, 6 models.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Some extraction faults: duplicated EP07 in the Fig 2 text; the Table 6 header columns are scrambled ("Origin" holds baseline accuracy and "Relative Gain" is absolute points, not a percentage); the Fig 1 numbers are not mappable to models; the Table 1 caption has garbled "++Ours". The headline 8.00% and 115% could not be tied to a specific Table 1 row, and the 19% and 12% TruthfulQA figures could not be derived from Table 3, so cite them as the paper's own claims. The venue is unverified; no venue was printed in the PDF. Note for the note: this is a pre-reasoning-model result, so frame it as a historical or weak technique with the caveats above.
